articles.headline: El INSS acumula en Lugo 1.629 expedientes de incapacidad sin resolver
articles.subtitle: El Gobierno responde a los senadores del PP que todos los trabajadores cobran una prestación mientras se tramita su caso, y los populares acusan al Ejecutivo de dejar las oficinas «al límite» por no reponer efectivos.
articles.body:
El Instituto Nacional de la Seguridad Social (INSS) tiene pendientes de resolver en la provincia de Lugo 1.629 expedientes de incapacidad permanente, según la respuesta del Gobierno a una pregunta registrada a principios de junio por los senadores del PP José Manuel Balseiro, José Manuel Barreiro y Juan Carlos Serrano.

Los senadores sostenían que la situación «continúa generando una creciente preocupación entre ciudadanos y trabajadores» por el aumento de los tiempos de espera, las dificultades para obtener atención presencial y el retraso acumulado en la tramitación de expedientes y prestaciones. El Ejecutivo replica que todos los trabajadores reciben una prestación mientras se resuelve su caso.

El PP atribuye el atasco a «una política de reducción y falta de reposición de efectivos» que, sostiene, está llevando a muchas oficinas a una situación límite y perjudica especialmente a las personas mayores y a quienes tienen más dificultades para relacionarse por vía telemática.

En junio los populares llevaron el asunto al Senado y reclamaron cubrir con urgencia las plazas de médicos evaluadores en Lugo, que describían como insuficientes ante lo que llamaron un «auténtico colapso» de la oficina provincial.

articles.headline: La Rúa Nova amanece otra vez con botellas y vasos, y los vecinos siguen pendientes del Valedor
articles.subtitle: Los residentes del casco histórico de Lugo ven confirmado su diagnóstico: el botellón vuelve cada fin de semana aunque no haya fiestas multitudinarias, y han pedido amparo al Valedor do Pobo por lo que sufren en las galerías de su edificio.
articles.body:
La Rúa Nova volvió a amanecer este domingo cubierta de botellas, vasos de plástico y de vidrio y otros residuos, una estampa que los vecinos describen ya como el día de la marmota. Los operarios de la concesionaria municipal retiraron la basura y baldearon la calle en las primeras horas de la mañana, pero el mal ya estaba hecho.

La noche no fue de las más concurridas de la capital, con fiestas como las de Paradai y O Parque pero ninguna de las multitudinarias, lo que para los afectados confirma que el problema no depende de citas concretas: el botellón en el entorno de las galerías se repite cada semana.

Los residentes han pedido amparo al Valedor do Pobo. En su escrito se declaran «cansados e fartos» de las consecuencias de unas reuniones que se celebran en un espacio privado y que se traducen, dicen, en cristales rotos, líquidos, orines, ruidos sin límite y personas al amanecer en estado vegetativo. Los vecinos advierten del riesgo que todo eso supone para los ocupantes de las viviendas, en buena parte personas mayores.

articles.headline: El PP acusa al Gobierno de «alentar» la entrada en Ceuta y el PSOE busca salida en los Presupuestos
articles.subtitle: Los populares sostienen que el Ejecutivo «pudo promover» aquel paso masivo, mientras los médicos de la ciudad alertan de que la sanidad va a colapsar y los socialistas admiten que las cuentas de 2027 son su única vía para cambiar de conversación.
articles.body:
La crisis política abierta por la entrada masiva de migrantes en Ceuta sigue sin salida a la vista. El PP sostiene que el Gobierno «pudo promover» aquel paso y lo acusa de estar «alentando próximas invasiones», una acusación que el Ejecutivo rechaza.

En el PSOE, varias voces admiten que hoy no hay números para aprobar los Presupuestos Generales del Estado, pero consideran su negociación «lo único que tenemos» para rebajar la tensión tras Ceuta. Algunas federaciones van más allá y ven en las cuentas, si se tumban, una rampa hacia unas elecciones a comienzos de 2027.

Mientras, en la ciudad, los médicos alertan de que la sanidad ceutí va a colapsar y piden trasladar a los migrantes a otro centro para liberar citas a los residentes. Este fin de semana un operativo reubicó a pie a unos 800 migrantes desde las calles hasta un centro de acogida, 45 días después de la entrada masiva.

articles.headline: Asesinada en Cuautla una estudiante española de intercambio, investigada como feminicidio
articles.subtitle: La víctima, de 21 años y natural de Salamanca, estudiaba un mes de intercambio en Morelos y fue atacada con arma blanca en un presunto asalto junto a la Casa de la Cultura, adonde había ido a una fiesta local.
articles.body:
Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, estudiante española de 21 años, murió la noche del sábado en un ataque con arma blanca en Cuautla, en el estado mexicano de Morelos. La agresión se produjo en un presunto asalto a las afueras de la Casa de la Cultura, adonde había acudido a la Fiesta Nacional de la Planta Medicinal.

El fiscal de Morelos, Fernando Blumenkron, explicó que el caso se investiga con el protocolo de feminicidio, que se agotarán todas las líneas de investigación y que la Fiscalía contactó de inmediato con el Consulado de España. La joven falleció antes de que llegaran los servicios de emergencia, y la policía buscaba a un hombre con sudadera blanca y mochila negra señalado por testigos.

Estudiaba en la Universidad de Granada y llevaba un mes de intercambio en la Universidad Autónoma del Estado de Morelos (UAEM), que ha exigido a las autoridades una investigación «inmediata, exhaustiva y con estricta perspectiva de género» para evitar la impunidad. La zona está bajo el operativo federal conocido como Plan Cuautla.

articles.headline: Cinco detenidos al embestir una narcolancha a una patrullera de la Guardia Civil en Almería
articles.subtitle: El choque ocurrió en la costa de Adra y dejó varios heridos, dos evacuados al hospital de Poniente y uno de los arrestados en la UCI, en un episodio que reaviva la alerta por la violencia del narcotráfico en la zona.
articles.body:
Una narcolancha embistió este domingo a una patrullera de la Guardia Civil en la costa de Adra, en Almería. El balance provisional es de cinco detenidos y varios heridos, dos de ellos evacuados al Hospital Universitario de Poniente, en El Ejido.

Otras fuentes próximas al caso elevan a tres el número de heridos entre los arrestados y sitúan a uno de ellos en la UCI. La Comandancia de Almería confirmó la colisión, pero no dio detalles sobre el estado de los implicados ni sobre cómo se produjo el impacto.

El episodio reaviva la alerta por la violencia del narcotráfico en la zona. Vega Romero advirtió de una «escalada» ligada a la entrada de cocaína y a la implantación de «mafias del Este y de América del Sur», un escenario que, según alertó, puede acabar derivando en el uso de «armas de guerra» como lanzacohetes.

articles.headline: Dos heridos y 9.500 confinados por el incendio de Benahavís, que avanza hacia Pujerra
articles.subtitle: El fuego, declarado en el paraje de la Ermita del Rosario, obligó a desalojar la urbanización Montemayor Alto y a enviar un aviso ES-Alert a los móviles de la zona, con 22 medios aéreos trabajando en su extinción.
articles.body:
Un incendio forestal declarado este domingo en el paraje de la Ermita del Rosario, en Benahavís (Málaga), obligó a confinar preventivamente el casco urbano de la localidad, de unos 9.500 habitantes, y a desalojar la urbanización Montemayor Alto, con medio centenar de vecinos.

El fuego, que avanza hacia Pujerra, dejó dos heridos —tres, según otras fuentes—: una persona con quemaduras al intentar apagar las llamas y un bombero forestal con traumatismos por una caída. El 112 recibió el primer aviso hacia las 12.40 horas y a las 13.41 se elevó el plan Infoca a fase de emergencia, situación operativa 1.

La Junta envió un mensaje ES-Alert, en español y en inglés, a los móviles de la zona, y pidió cerrar puertas y ventanas y proteger a niños, mayores y enfermos por el humo. El confinamiento alcanza también a diseminados del norte y el oeste y a la urbanización La Coja, mientras los efectivos tratan de fijar el perímetro.

articles.headline: Little-Pengelly accuses O'Neill of 'weaponising' First Minister role ahead of Cardiff summit
articles.subtitle: The DUP deputy First Minister says Sinn Féin's leader has no authority to sign anything as First Minister at Monday's meeting of the three nationalist leaders, where a referendum memorandum is expected.
articles.body:
The First Ministers of Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales meet in Cardiff on Monday, the first face-to-face meeting of the three nationalist leaders since Plaid Cymru's Rhun ap Iorwerth took office in May. Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald will also attend.

An agreement on collaboration, expected to include a memorandum of understanding on pushing for referendums, is due to be signed, with the leaders attending as party leaders rather than as government officials. DUP deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly said Michelle O'Neill had "not sought any agreement or permission from me to travel, attend or sign anything as First Minister", and accused her of trying to weaponise the role. She added that the two roles at Stormont are "entirely joint roles".

Ap Iorwerth said the meeting was about working more closely on shared interests, including fair funding and "a different attitude from UK government".

It follows Donald Trump's weekend remarks in support of Irish unity, which pushed the border poll question into the spotlight, and Scottish education secretary Mairi McAllan's insistence that an independence referendum is "not off the table". The prime minister has said a vote could follow a "clear consensus" in Scotland, but a letter to John Swinney later clarified that a referendum remains "off limits".

articles.headline: Sweden's centre-left bloc edges ahead as the election count goes to the wire
articles.subtitle: With almost every district counted, the four-party alliance led by Magdalena Andersson holds 176 seats against 173 for the governing right, leaving the result dependent on late postal votes.
articles.body:
Sweden's centre-left bloc edged ahead as the count neared its end, with 176 seats for the four-party alliance led by the Social Democrats against 173 for the governing right once almost all districts had reported.

The campaign was dominated by immigration, which the government has spent years tightening, and by support for Ukraine, where Sweden has become one of Kyiv's most dependable backers. The far-right Sweden Democrats, who keep the government in office without sitting in it, were poised for their first losses under Jimmie Åkesson even as he pressed to enter a cabinet.

Postal and overseas votes will be counted until Wednesday at the earliest, and the race remains close enough that neither side has claimed victory. Magdalena Andersson wants a four-party coalition with the Greens and the Left, while the governing parties have spent the weekend warning that a red-green budget would undo their migration reforms.

articles.headline: Russian drone hits passenger train minutes after Boris Johnson's party leaves border station
articles.subtitle: Kyiv and Warsaw call the strike on a Kyiv-Warsaw service an escalation, saying the train was hit two kilometres from Poland while the former prime minister and Western advisers were travelling through the region.
articles.body:
A Russian drone struck a passenger train in western Ukraine on Sunday, in an attack that Kyiv and Warsaw described as an escalation and that turned a border journey into a security scare for Boris Johnson, who was travelling in the region with parliamentary advisers from several European countries. No casualties were reported, and the former CIA director David Petraeus had been on an earlier train through the same station.

Ukraine's national rail operator said the train on the Kyiv-Warsaw route was hit about two kilometres from the Polish border, minutes after the group's train had left a border station. Johnson was reported to be unharmed.

The strike put fresh attention on Ukraine's rail network, a repeated target of Russian attacks, and on the risk of the war spilling across Nato's eastern edge. In Washington, Donald Trump has been pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries, wary of taking Russian diesel out of global markets and pushing up fuel prices at home.

articles.headline: Deaths and more than 100 missing after Indonesian ferry capsizes
articles.subtitle: Rescuers pulled 107 people from the sea after the Virgo Transport 8, carrying 243 passengers and crew, overturned in bad weather, with the search continuing for those still unaccounted for.
articles.body:
An Indonesian ferry carrying 243 passengers and crew capsized in bad weather, and more than 100 people were still unaccounted for as rescuers continued their search. Authorities said 107 people had been rescued and 27 bodies recovered, while earlier reports put the death toll at six and the number missing at about 130.

The transport minister, Dudy Purwagandhi, said the vessel had lost contact with its owners and that waves of up to 2.5 metres had been reported in the area. Fishing boats joined the search, and a survivor described the moment the ship overturned.

Indonesia's islands depend on ferries, and the archipelago has a long record of deadly sinkings. The accident came as authorities warned of high seas in the region, with rescue crews working through the night.

articles.headline: Israeli culture minister moves to strip NAZA filmmakers of citizenship after Venice prize
articles.subtitle: Miki Zohar called the documentary about Israel's war in Gaza "vile" and its Special Jury Prize "shocking", accusing directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor of treason against the state.
articles.body:
Israel's culture minister, Miki Zohar, said he will move to revoke the Israeli citizenship of filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor after their documentary NAZA won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival. In a post on X on Sunday he called the film "vile" and its win "shocking", accused the directors of harming the country "just to get applause from antisemites around the world", and said their actions "constitute treason against the state".

The 80-minute film documents Israel's use of AI-powered systems in Gaza and received a 25-minute standing ovation at its premiere. It draws on testimony from Israeli military and intelligence personnel who spoke anonymously and described "Lavender", a system used to monitor communications between Palestinians and identify targets for killing, according to the festival's synopsis. Abraham said he hoped the documentary would push Western governments to apply economic sanctions on Israel.

articles.headline: Trump says he will take US tariffs off Irish whiskey
articles.subtitle: The US president announced the move during the Irish Open at Doonbeg, County Clare, a day after the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, raised the duty with him at Farmleigh.
articles.body:
Donald Trump has said he will take US tariffs off Irish whiskey. The announcement came during his weekend visit to Doonbeg, County Clare, for the Irish Open, after the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, raised the duty with him the previous day at Farmleigh.

Whiskey is among Ireland's most exposed exports to the United States, and the tariff has been a standing complaint for distillers since it was imposed. Martin has made the issue a fixture of his contacts with Washington, and the drinks industry welcomed the president's remarks.

Trump's visit also drew attention for his reiteration of support for Irish unity, remarks that thrust the question of a border poll into the spotlight on the eve of Monday's meeting of the three nationalist first ministers in Cardiff.

articles.headline: Apple is designing its own iPhone game controller, reports say
articles.subtitle: The company is said to be working on a dedicated pad and a holder that turns the phone into a handheld console, with the project led from its Beats brand and third-party accessory makers in its sights.
articles.body:
Apple is designing its own game controllers for the iPhone, according to reports, in a push to turn the phone into a handheld console rather than leaving players to buy third-party pads. The project is reportedly being run from within Beats, the brand Apple has used for accessories pitched at a more mainstream audience than its own gear.

The reports describe a dedicated controller as well as a holder that pairs the phone with the pad, giving games a fixed physical interface instead of touch controls. Apple has spent years courting developers with console-grade chips in its phones and a growing catalogue of premium titles that are awkward to play without a gamepad.

If the plans go ahead, the accessories would compete directly with pads from established makers and tighten Apple's grip on a gaming market it already monetises through the App Store. Apple has not commented, and the reports do not give a launch date.

articles.headline: iOS 27 arrives on Tuesday — minus two features Apple had already promised
articles.subtitle: The update brings a wave of Apple Intelligence changes to the iPhone, but two headline additions have slipped to a later release and not every recent handset will be able to install it.
articles.body:
Apple will release iOS 27 for the iPhone on Tuesday, closing out a bumpy year for its software and its AI features. The update went out to developers and testers over the summer, and users install it through Settings, with Apple urging them to back up first.

The release arrives with a long list of Apple Intelligence additions, but not everything the company showed off: two features will not be ready until a future software update, a pattern that has dogged the company's AI roadmap since iOS 26. Reviewers have also been working through interface changes that 9to5Mac described as breaking 15 years of muscle memory on the iPhone and iPad.

Not every iPhone will get the update, and users on older handsets will be left behind. Apple is rolling the download out by time zone during the day.

articles.headline: Federighi answers the awkward question about the iPhone Duo and the iPad
articles.subtitle: Apple's software chief has addressed the overlap between its new folding phone and its tablet, as reviewers praise the Duo's split screen and conclude that iPad multitasking now feels convoluted by comparison.
articles.body:
Apple's new folding iPhone has forced the company to explain how a phone that opens into a small tablet differs from the iPad. Software chief Craig Federighi addressed the overlap directly, in remarks reported by 9to5Mac, as reviewers compared the two devices side by side.

The verdict from early testing is mixed in an instructive way: the iPhone Duo's split-screen behaviour has been judged well executed, while the iPad's multitasking looks convoluted next to it. The Duo's split view deliberately does not work like the tablet's, and the handset arrives without some features that Apple's other flagships offer.

Columnists expect a wider shift. The Duo is widely read as Apple's attempt to make folding phones the norm rather than a novelty, and analysts expect it to drive an upgrade cycle that lifts iPhone demand — and prices — through the coming quarters.

articles.headline: StarCraft returns in 2030 as an open-world shooter
articles.subtitle: Blizzard used BlizzCon to announce a new StarCraft, a decade after the last game and more than a decade after the cancelled spinoff that would have taken the series in the same direction.
articles.body:
Blizzard has announced a new StarCraft, coming in 2030 as an open-world shooter — a genre shift for a series that helped define real-time strategy. The reveal came at BlizzCon, where the company also ran through news for Diablo, Overwatch and World of Warcraft.

The choice revives an approach Blizzard abandoned years ago, when a StarCraft shooter was cancelled mid-development. This time the project is being announced with a release year attached, and with the studio's wider slate positioned around it.

StarCraft has been dormant since 2015, and its return gives Blizzard a flagship franchise to lean on at a moment when its release schedule has been thin. The company has not said which platforms the game will reach.

articles.headline: Larry Ellison calls off a $7.5bn sale of Oracle stock
articles.subtitle: The co-founder scrapped the planned offload days after Oracle's shares came under pressure, with the company trying to convince investors that its AI spending will pay off rather than destroy its software business.
articles.body:
Larry Ellison has cancelled a plan to sell up to $7.5 billion worth of Oracle stock, according to filings reported by CNBC and TechCrunch. The decision removes a large block of shares from the market at a sensitive moment for the company.

Oracle has had a bruising stretch, with its share price hit as investors questioned the returns on the data-centre build-out it has funded to serve AI customers. Executives have spent weeks arguing the opposite case, insisting that AI will rescue Oracle's software business rather than upend it.

Ellison's personal stake in the company has become a market story in itself, and the cancelled sale is likely to be read as a signal about his own view of the shares. Neither Oracle nor Ellison has explained the reversal.

articles.headline: Trump and Johnson wave away the slowdown plea from the AI labs' own bosses
articles.subtitle: The president said the technology should keep advancing and the House speaker treated the warnings as an overreaction, hours after the heads of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX urged governments to be ready to put the brakes on.
articles.body:
Donald Trump has dismissed calls to slow down artificial intelligence, saying the technology should be allowed to keep advancing, after the leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX jointly urged governments to be ready to pace the development of increasingly capable systems. The intervention from the labs' own bosses was striking because it came from companies with the most to gain from speed.

The dismissal went beyond the White House. The House speaker, Mike Johnson, also pushed back on the idea of a slowdown, even as a bipartisan group of senators pressed the case for rules on the technology.

Washington is now scrambling to respond, with the window for legislation this year narrowing as members prepare to leave for the midterm campaign. Industry figures on both sides of the argument appear to be betting that the election, rather than Congress, will decide how much rulemaking actually lands.

articles.headline: Anthropic's bioweapons warning divides the researchers it was meant to alarm
articles.subtitle: The company says users found ways around its safeguards while probing bioweapons research, and argues the industry should slow down; some scientists call that a chilling confirmation, others an overreaction built on thin evidence.
articles.body:
Anthropic's account of how users circumvented its safety systems while researching bioweapons has split the research community. Some scientists have treated the disclosure as a chilling demonstration of how quickly guardrails can be probed, while others have dismissed it as an overreaction resting on a handful of cases that prove less than the company claims.

The report also described kamikaze drone swarms and other misuse, and Anthropic used the findings to argue for a slower pace of development — an argument critics say conveniently serves the company's own competitive position. Ars Technica reported a similar pattern of workarounds found by users of its Claude models.

The argument has landed while the United States, Britain and the European Union weigh new rules, and as researchers disagree about how much weight to give evaluations run by the companies themselves. Science canvassed specialists on both sides of that question.

articles.headline: Obama tells Democrats to arrive at the AI fight with a plan
articles.subtitle: The former president used a fundraiser to push for clear AI safeguards and to press House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries to put oversight at the centre of the party's midterm argument.
articles.body:
Barack Obama has pressed Democrats to make artificial intelligence oversight a central part of their pitch, telling a fundraiser that the party needs a clear plan for safeguards rather than a set of slogans. He also called on House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries to put the issue at the heart of the agenda.

The party has been splintered on how far to go. Some Democrats want new agencies and licensing rules for frontier models, others prefer transparency mandates and liability for the harm AI causes. Obama's intervention, reported by Politico, The Hill, CNBC and TechCrunch, gives the stricter camp its most senior voice so far.

Jeffries has said Democrats will meet on the subject on Tuesday, days before the House leaves Washington for the campaign. Republicans, led by the president, are arguing that the industry should be left alone, which leaves the party's position on AI as one of the clearest dividing lines going into the midterms.

articles.headline: Anthropic chooses Nasdaq for its listing while its CEO asks the industry to slow down
articles.subtitle: The company is preparing one of the year's biggest offerings, expects adjusted operating profit this quarter and is reported to be working towards a valuation near $2tn, even as it argues frontier development should be paced.
articles.body:
Anthropic will list on Nasdaq, Bloomberg reported, as the AI developer prepares one of the largest offerings of the year. The company is said to be meeting investors, and the Financial Times reported that it expects adjusted operating profit this quarter — a milestone few frontier labs have reached.

Reports put its ambitions around a $2 trillion valuation, a figure that sits awkwardly beside its chief executive's public argument that the industry should pace development rather than race towards the most capable models. CNBC described the strategy as a tightrope walk: pursuing an offering while pushing for a slowdown.

Critics have gone further. The Register read the company's safety-first framing as a bid to write rules that would constrain smaller competitors, calling it a set of terms for regulatory capture dressed up as pacing the frontier. Anthropic has not responded publicly to that characterisation.

articles.headline: Z.ai's share slide shows the cost of China's model race
articles.subtitle: The developer's shares fell more than 10% after it raised about $5bn in a second fundraising in two months, while DeepSeek's latest model showed how much capability can be squeezed out of far less compute.
articles.body:
Shares in Z.ai fell more than 10% after the Chinese developer raised about $5 billion, its second major fundraising in two months, with investors questioning the cash burn behind the country's model race. Bloomberg reported that the appetite for such deals has driven an Alibaba-style wave of listings in Hong Kong.

The fundraising tells only half the story. DeepSeek's newest model has been described by The Register as a template for powerful language models that run lean, a reminder that Chinese labs are competing on efficiency as much as on sheer scale and spending.

Beijing's own rhetoric has shifted too. China's spy chief warned about the risks posed by the technology in the same week that American executives called for the brakes to be applied, a combination that is reshaping how governments frame the race.
